Hundreds Evacuated from Oleshky Amid Rare Russia‑Ukraine Ceasefire, Media Say

02 Nov 2026, 02:22 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Editorial Desk · Source: timesofindia.indiatimes.com

Image: The Times of India · Photo source · Resized and letterboxed to 16:9; no AI generation

Key takeaways Overview - A humanitarian evacuation took place on **Friday** from the Russian‑occupied Ukrainian town of **Oleshky**. - According to multiple media outlets, the operation was carried out under a **temporary cease‑fire** that had been in effect across the Kherson fron

Overview

  • A humanitarian evacuation took place on Friday from the Russian‑occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
  • According to multiple media outlets, the operation was carried out under a temporary cease‑fire that had been in effect across the Kherson front since Tuesday.

Reported Details

  • Transport route: Residents were reportedly moved by bus through the Crimean peninsula to the Russian Black‑Sea resort of Anapa, then flown on three aircraft to Gomel, Belarus. From there they are expected to cross into Ukraine via a Belarus‑Ukraine border checkpoint.
  • Scale: A convoy of 25 buses was said to have been deployed, with a capacity to move up to 750 people. Ambulances were on standby for those with limited mobility.
  • Timing: Evacuees were given a four‑hour window on Friday, with the last flight landing in Gomel on Saturday.
  • Cease‑fire context: The BBC described the cease‑fire covering the Kherson region as the longest and most extensive since Russia’s full‑scale invasion began in 2022.

Confirmed Statements

  • Russian human‑rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova (as quoted by Belta) said the evacuation “unfolded without any incidents” and praised the “high level of organisation”.
  • Ukrainian authorities confirmed that evacuees were first taken to southern Russia before proceeding to Ukraine via Belarus.
  • BBC and Reuters both reported that the operation was the first joint humanitarian effort of its kind in four years and eight months of the conflict.

Unverified or Disputed Claims

  • Some outlets, including the Times of India, attribute the cease‑fire negotiation to U.S. First Lady Melania Trump. No official statement from the White House or the U.S. State Department has been identified to corroborate this claim.
  • The exact number of people evacuated varies between reports ("hundreds" vs. "up to 750"). Independent verification on the ground has not been published.
  • Claims that the road out of Oleshky was cleared of landmines during the cease‑fire have not been independently confirmed.

Practical Implications

  • Humanitarian access: If the corridor remains open, additional aid deliveries and civilian movements could be coordinated, potentially easing the humanitarian situation in Kherson.
  • Security considerations: Both sides will need to maintain the cease‑fire to prevent accidental engagements, especially around the transport routes through Crimea and Belarus.
  • Diplomatic signal: Even if the involvement of a U.S. figure is unverified, the reported cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials could be a tentative step toward broader de‑escalation.

How to Verify

  • Official statements: Check the websites of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence, the Russian Ministry of Defence, and the Belarusian State News Agency (Belta) for press releases.
  • Independent monitors: Look for updates from the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission to Ukraine or NGOs such as International Committee of the Red Cross.
  • Satellite imagery: Open‑source satellite services can confirm the presence of aircraft at Gomel airport and the movement of buses on the reported routes.
  • Local reporting: Regional journalists in Kherson and Oleshky may provide on‑the‑ground accounts once the area is accessible.

Sources

  • BBC News (online report, 2024)
  • Reuters (wire service, 2024)
  • Belta – Belarusian State News Agency (press release, 2024)
